messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Mean structure question
parts:
There are a couple of options. The measurementInvariance function will return a list of lavaan objects (one for each model fit). For example if you ran the following code:

fit<-measurementInvariance(HW.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, group="school")

The object fit would be a list of 4 lavaan objects (corresponding to configural, weak, strong and latent mean invariance). You could examine any of the models by looking at an element in the list.

For example 
summary(fit[[3]]) #this is a summary of the strong invariance model
summary(fit[[4]]) #this is a summary of the mean invariant model

Alternatively you could use the group.equal option in any of the lavaan functions (cfa, sem, growth or lavaan) to accomplish the same thing.

Alex

messages.author: 5d4f9e7f97c21008
messages.subject: Re: Mean structure question
parts:
Ah yes. Within the summaries of individual models the latent means should be reported (look under the Intercepts section). Specifically if you save the results from measurementInvariance as an object the third element of that list (e.g. fit[[3]]) from above, contains the estimates of latent means (with the first group set to 0). Now by default lavaan will set the scale of the model by fixing the first factor loading to 1 and the means in the first group to 0. If you want to set the scale a different way, then the syntax gets a bit more complex.

I should also mention that the same results can be obtained by fitting models using the group.equal argument in any of the lavaan functions (cfa, sem, growth, lavaan). By setting group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts") you will fit a strong invariant model.

Hope that helps.

Alex

messages.author: c1e1212cf2e076c1
messages.subject: Re: Mean structure question
parts: I'm trying to run measurement invariance for my factor model that has ordered categorical outcomes (1 through 5), using the ordered statement. Lavaan doesn't seem to create item intercepts when using the ordered statement. Any insight into why this may be? If it is for statistical purposes, how can I measure strong invariance or scalar invariance (using Vandenberg's terminology) without the intercepts?

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Mean structure question
parts:
Hi Robin

When you are using ordered variables, intercepts are not estimated, what is estimated instead are thresholds. So, for example if a variable have 3 categories it will have 2 thresholds.

The syntax for thresholds would be:

var | t1 ## indicating the first threshold for the variable var

If you are using the "group.equal" argument in the cfa function you can add "thresholds" instead of intercepts. If you are doing it by syntax you can do the next:

var1 | c(th1,th1)*t1 
var1 | c(th2,th2)*t2

var2 | c(th3,th3)*t1
var2 | c(th4,th4)*t1

this will constraint the 2 thresholds for variables var1 and var2 equal across 2 groups.

hope it helps

 -Mauricio

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Mean structure question
parts: For a follow-up question, if I want to convert these mean differences to a Cohen's d-type effect size, would I just divide the mean difference by the square root of the variance of the latent for my non-reference group?

It depends.  Actual Cohen's d is divided by the square-root of the pooled variance (use the same as for the t test formula for unequal Ns/variances).  Glass' delta was developed with treatment-control designs in mind, and it divides by the control-group's SD, because treatments can change the spread as well as the location of data.  I would be inclined to use the reference group's SD, since that group (with latent M = 0) is the reference group to which you are comparing the latent M = -0.71

If you test whether latent variances can be constrained to equality and cannot reject the null, then you only have one SD to work with, which would make the choice simpler.

Terry

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Mean structure question
parts: When I obtain the means from the summary(fit.invariance[[3]]), all the means have different estimates. How would I get the estimates for the means that are constrained across groups?
You can find them in the constrained model, which was used to test whether those constraints are tenable:  fit.invariance[[4]] (or fit.invariance[[5]] if you set strict = FALSE)
As mentioned previously, the summary(cfa.fit) will only give 0.000 for the mean estimates of the latents, even when using group.equal=c("means","intercepts").

The default method for identifying the mean structure with latent variables is to set the latent means/intercepts to zero (regardless of whether std.lv = TRUE or FALSE).  When you constrain indicator intercepts to equality across groups, that allows you to estimate all but 1 of the groups' latent means.  To test whether the latent means are the same, you constrain them to equality -- because you need to identify the latent means, constraining them to equality means constraining them to all == 0.  You can estimate equality-constrained latent means if you identify them by choosing a reference indicator and set its intercept (across groups) to zero.  But ultimately, that just makes your latent means equal to (equality-constrained) indicator means.  You could also use the effects-coding method of identification (constrain the indicator intercepts to average 0, so you can estimate all intercepts and latent means), but the location of an unobserved distribution on the real-number line is arbitrary, so I don't think it buys you any interpretability to constrain estimated latent means instead of constraining them all to a fixed quantity.

Terry
